title: Nether Beast Character Study: Staying on The Mark (13/22)
summary: Third part of NH's character study of the YouTuber Nether Beast, whom he considers a fraudulent fake natty. He catalogs lies (curing COVID with herbs, ET DNA, a 500 lb weighted pull-up), criticizes his program sales and bad advice, and argues that a 50-60 lb muscle loss and quick gains prove past PED use, using him as a template for spotting deception across YouTube fitness.
claims: NH makes character studies of fitness YouTubers he considers fraudulent, misinforming or pathological liars, basing every claim on verifiable content from their own channels
Nutrition is not a magic pill: it matters for longevity but has significant limits for building a body or fighting
Claiming to have cured COVID-19 with garden herbs is implausible: if a herb worked, others with medicinal gardens would have found it too
Most people selling programs on YouTube are scam artists; learn to program for yourself instead of paying them
Copy-paste programs sent at random to paying clients are a scam
Training a single body part with 25-rep sets of one exercise is how drug users train; naturals get nothing from it
Fitness sellers use urgency marketing (limited offer, first come first served) because scarcity makes people want things they did not need
Paid one-on-one calls let bad coaches avoid public scrutiny: clueless clients cannot judge or record the advice, unlike a free public video that can be corrected in the comments

Crushing your wrists with a bolt tightener to create microfractures and thicken them is terrible advice: unlike shins, wrists are joints, and calcifying them limits range of motion and can wreck your pressing and curling for life
Gurus who try to get followers to come live with them on an island reproduce a cult pattern that always ends with the followers being used
A claim that humans carry extraterrestrial DNA proven by peer-reviewed papers would be the biggest scientific news in a century; it is absent because it is false
Real fighters throw punches by rotating the hips, not from the elbow, and kick with one leg planted; flying kicks are almost never seen in the UFC
PEDs tend to make users more aggressive and lower the voice; a sudden change in mood and voice when someone resumes bodybuilding is suspicious
Wearing very baggy clothes when at your biggest can be a sign of bigorexia, which PED use worsens, and can hide muscle lost between cycles
Most fitness YouTubers share the same deception patterns as extreme frauds, so learning to spot them in one helps you spot them in all
You should not give authoritative advice on training a body part that is clearly weak on you; applying the theory matters as much as the theory
Calling squats and deadlifts useless for legs while having chicken legs, even on PEDs, discredits leg advice
Liars about strength go straight for world-record numbers instead of believable ones, like a 500 lb weighted pull-up
A one-arm pull-up is not just twice as hard as a two-arm pull-up; it is exponentially harder because body angle and movement change
Small YouTubers who only associate with smaller, skinny novices do it to build a hierarchy of followers who cannot expose them
Anyone following a program centered on compound movements with discipline already has the potential to look better than a fraudulent guru
50-60 lb of solid muscle takes a natural lifter decades to build; someone who trained for years would never let it waste away
Muscle memory only means part of lost muscle returns faster; after 10 years of training and a full detrain, it takes much longer than a year to come back
Being small in 2014-2015 then huge by 2017 and later losing it all is a PED pattern, not 20 years of natural building
People who downplay the effects of PEDs are often users themselves; PEDs build muscle even without training
A natural cannot outdo a long-term PED user in size with mental strength; long enough PED use guarantees a big body, though not a good-looking one
Some PED users convince themselves they are natural because they believe the drugs only gave them the gains their years of poor training deserved
Using steroids to replace hard work, programming, diet, or perceived missing genetics is not natural; it is cowardly
Physique content (flexing, abs thumbnails) is the easiest way to grow a fitness channel; an abs flex video gets NH around 10,000 views
People wrongly equate a good physique with knowing how to train; drugs break that link because someone who cannot train or eat can still get big
Muscle makes a newcomer MMA fighter easier to promote, which can motivate PED use
